Efficient frontier with short sales

Mixes of A and B from 150% short in A to 250% short in B, true parameters. Solid is efficient, dashed is dominated, the green dot is the minimum-variance portfolio (MVP).

Efficient frontiers for all cases

Efficient branch of each preset correlation, short sales allowed. The thick line is the slider's choice.

Weekly returns of A against B

All 500 weeks. Drag a rectangle on the chart to zoom into it; double-click or press Reset to return.

Cumulative returns

Sum of weekly returns over 500 weeks. The MVP line mixes A and B with sample weights and no short sales.

Capital allocation line

Add a risk-free asset to the two risky ones. The line from the risk-free rate through a risky portfolio is its capital allocation line (CAL). Its slope is the Sharpe ratio, the price of one unit of risk. It uses the correlation set by the slider at the top.

Frontier, tangency portfolio and CAL

Solid red line: reachable CALs through the tangency portfolio T. Dotted lines: CALs of A and B alone, always flatter. A point further out the line, like L in the notes, needs borrowing.

What the numbers say

Tangency portfolio T is the risky mix with the highest Sharpe ratio. Everyone holds the same T whatever their risk aversion, and only the split between T and the risk-free asset differs.

Sharpe ratioValueCAL through
Your portfolioWeightReading

  • On the CAL: volatility is x times the volatility of T, and the expected return is rf + x (μT − rf). Risk is a straight-line function of how much you hold.
  • Beyond T (x above 100%): you borrow at rf and invest more than 100% in risky assets. Turn borrowing off and the line is dashed there.
  • Short selling: it lets T have weights below 0% or above 100% in A, which can raise the Sharpe ratio. With it off, T is the best mix inside 0% to 100%.

Preset cases

The five assignment correlations plus the extremes from the notes. Click a row to select it.

True ρSample ρ Mean AMean B Vol AVol B MVP A, shortMVP vol, short MVP A, no shortMVP vol, no short

True parameters: A has mean 15% and volatility 20%, B has mean 25% and volatility 30%, as in the lecture example. Weekly returns are normal with mean/52 and volatility/√52, using the same random shocks for every correlation, so changing ρ changes only the dependence. MVP weight in A = (σB² − σAB) / (σA² + σB² − 2σAB). At ρ = +1 this is 300% in A and −200% in B (σ = 0, return −5%); at ρ = −1 it is 60% in A (σ = 0, return 19%).
